explanation:
The principal contrast is storage versus thermogenesis. White adipose tissue stores triacylglycerols and also has endocrine functions, whereas brown adipose tissue is specialized for heat production. Assigning all adipose tissue the same role would erase that distinction.

Separate the main storage role from the additional signaling role. White adipose tissue stores fuel as triacylglycerol, but it is not merely an inert container: the course also emphasizes endocrine functions. Brown adipose tissue is the contrasting thermogenic example linked to UCP1-rich mitochondria. The alternatives about producing all eicosanoids or specifically thromboxane do not define white adipose tissue. The correct choice is broad enough to include both functions highlighted by the lecture, without making every adipocyte equally thermogenic or assigning every lipid-related pathway to the same tissue.

Brown adipocytes contain many mitochondria equipped with thermogenin. Proton return through that protein releases more gradient energy as heat instead of capturing it in ATP. This explains why thermogenesis, rather than glycogen storage or DNA replication, is the defining function here.

Brown adipose tissue contains abundant mitochondria with thermogenin/UCP1. That protein provides a route for proton return that bypasses ATP synthase, allowing a greater share of respiratory energy to be dissipated as heat. Thermogenesis therefore connects the tissue's specialized function with the mitochondrial mechanism from Week 10. DNA replication and protein secretion are not the distinguishing adaptations being asked about, while glycogen storage misses both the lipid context and the heat-producing role. The answer should be selected for the tissue's emphasized specialization, not simply for a process that cells can perform.

The distinguishing word is inducible: beige adipocytes can acquire a thermogenic role in response to stimulation. That differs from describing them simply as ordinary white-fat storage cells or as cells without mitochondria. The lecture's comparison concerns regulation of their heat-producing capacity.

The important word is **inducible**: the lecture distinguishes beige adipocytes by their capacity to develop a thermogenic function in the relevant setting. This is not the same description as white fat's main storage/endocrine role or the emphasized thermogenic specialization of brown fat. Absence of mitochondria would conflict with the mitochondrial basis of this heat production. Inability to store lipids and constitutive COX-2 expression are not the defining properties supplied by the lecture. Keep the comparison at the stated level rather than adding unprovided triggers or developmental mechanisms.

A cis double bond bends the fatty-acid chain, making neighboring tails pack less tightly. The physical effect follows from chain shape rather than a loss of all hydrophobic character. This structural reasoning connects unsaturation with lipid properties.

The cis arrangement changes the shape of the hydrocarbon chain by introducing a bend. Bent chains cannot align and pack as tightly as straighter chains in the comparison used here. The structural change therefore helps explain a physical property rather than changing the molecule into another class of nutrient. A double bond does not convert a fatty acid into carbohydrate or remove all its hydrophobic character. The straightening option reverses the stated effect. Begin with the local chain shape, then infer its consequence for how neighboring chains fit together.

Essential refers to a dietary requirement, not merely to a molecule being useful. The organism needs the fatty acid but cannot synthesize it adequately to meet that need. Its location in a cell or absence of double bonds is not what defines essentiality.

Essential has a specific nutritional meaning in this question. The organism requires the fatty acid, but endogenous synthesis does not supply the needed kind or amount, so dietary intake is necessary. Merely being useful, being found in mitochondria, or lacking double bonds does not establish essentiality. The option claiming unlimited synthesis would remove the reason for the dietary requirement. This distinction matters when comparing the named essential fatty acids with other important lipids: biological importance alone is not enough to place every useful fatty acid in the essential category.

The course identifies linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid as the required dietary pair. The names are similar, so check that both appear rather than substituting a common saturated fatty acid. Their omega-6 and omega-3 classifications provide an additional distinction.

The two names to connect to the course definition are **linoleic acid** and **α-linolenic acid**. Their essential status concerns the requirement for dietary supply, not simply their being fatty acids. Linoleic acid belongs to the omega-6 family, while α-linolenic acid belongs to omega-3 in the lecture's comparison. The other options list different fatty acids or cholesterol and therefore do not reproduce the emphasized pair. Be careful with the similar names: the α-linolenic member is not interchangeable with linoleic acid, even though both are part of the dietary requirement discussed.

Omega numbering deliberately starts at the terminal methyl end of the fatty acid. Counting from the carboxyl end uses the wrong reference point for this name. Always establish the counting direction before locating the first double bond.

A fatty-acid chain has two distinguishable ends, and the naming convention determines which one supplies the starting point. Omega numbering starts at the terminal methyl end, not at the carboxyl group. From there, the omega number identifies the position of the first double bond. Counting from the wrong end can therefore give a different answer even when the molecular drawing is unchanged. A phosphate group is not the reference point for this fatty-acid convention. Always identify the methyl end before trying to classify a chain as omega-3 or omega-6.

The number three identifies the position of the first double bond when counted from the methyl end. More precisely, that bond is between carbons 3 and 4 from that end. It does not mean that the molecule has three double bonds in total.

Begin at the terminal methyl carbon and count inward along the chain. For omega-3, the first double bond is between the third and fourth carbons from that end. The number three specifies this position; it does not mean three total double bonds or three carbons from the carboxyl group. Six carbons from the methyl end would describe omega-6 instead. The option fixing the bond at carbon 20 has no basis in the naming rule. Stating both the reference end and the bond position makes the answer unambiguous.

Eicosanoids are lipid-derived signals, not storage carbohydrates or proteins. Their 20-carbon framework and derivation from polyunsaturated fatty acids explain the description. Their biological importance lies in signaling functions such as inflammation and clotting.

The correct description combines chemical origin and function. Eicosanoids are lipid-derived, 20-carbon signaling molecules formed from polyunsaturated fatty-acid precursors in the course's account. They participate in responses such as inflammation and clotting rather than serving as the enzyme that produces ATP. A membrane protein and a storage polysaccharide belong to different molecular categories. Do not confuse the signaling product with the enzymes that synthesize it. The later prostaglandin/TxA2 pathway is a detailed example within the broader eicosanoid family, not the definition of every possible family member's synthetic route.

Prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes all belong to the eicosanoid family discussed in the lecture. Therefore the inclusive choice is required rather than selecting only one valid example. Family membership does not mean that every member is made through the same COX branch.

Evaluate each named category before deciding whether all of the above is justified. Prostaglandins, thromboxanes, and leukotrienes are all included among the eicosanoids discussed by the course, so none of the individual entries excludes the others. Their common family membership does not imply identical functions or identical biosynthetic branches. In particular, the COX pathway examined in detail for prostaglandins and TxA2 should not automatically be assigned to every leukotriene. The correct answer concerns classification into the family, whereas the pathway-specific distinctions are a separate question.

In the pathway examined here, arachidonic acid is the fatty acid supplied to PGH synthase. It precedes PGH2 and the final prostaglandin or thromboxane products. Cholesterol or acetyl-CoA may matter elsewhere in lipid biology but is not this immediate pathway substrate.

Trace the pathway from precursor release to enzyme substrate. Arachidonic acid is released from membrane phospholipid and enters the PGHS/COX step that leads to PGH2 and then cell-specific prostaglandins or TxA2. Palmitate, acetate, and cholesterol are not the immediate fatty-acid substrate identified for this pathway in the lecture. The word immediate prevents substituting a broadly related metabolic precursor or another lipid. Also distinguish arachidonic acid from PGH2: the former enters PGHS, while the latter is produced by that enzyme step.

The first step frees the precursor from a membrane phospholipid. Phospholipase A2 performs that release, making arachidonic acid available for the subsequent COX/PGHS step. Confusing these enzymes would skip the distinction between precursor release and conversion to PGH2.

Identify the event being asked about: freeing arachidonic acid from its membrane-phospholipid form. Phospholipase A2 performs that release step in the course diagram. PGHS then acts on the available arachidonic acid downstream, so precursor release and intermediate synthesis are different enzyme jobs. The alternative enzymes belong to lactate metabolism, oxidative ATP synthesis, and glucose phosphorylation; none describes this phospholipid cleavage. Following the substrate's location before and after the reaction makes the enzyme choice meaningful instead of merely a memorized association with inflammation.

PGHS is the enzyme and PGH2 is the unstable product formed in the course pathway. Cell-specific enzymes act afterward to make particular prostaglandins or TxA2. Similar names should not obscure this enzyme–product distinction.

The similar names are the main trap. **PGH synthase**, abbreviated PGHS, is the enzyme, while **PGH2** is the intermediate produced in the pathway. Arachidonic acid is the substrate that enters that step, and cell-specific enzymes subsequently convert PGH2 into particular products. Linoleic acid is one of the essential fatty acids discussed earlier, NADH is an electron carrier, and acetyl-CoA is a metabolic acetyl carrier. None is the named output of PGHS in this sequence. Reading enzyme, substrate, and product as separate roles prevents a label-based guess.

Different cells can share an upstream intermediate yet express different downstream enzymes. Those enzymes determine which final eicosanoid is made. A pathway diagram with many branches is therefore not evidence that every branch operates in every cell.

A pathway overview combines possible branches, but a particular cell expresses only its own set of relevant enzymes. Two cells can share the upstream capacity to make PGH2 while converting that common intermediate into different downstream products. Platelet thromboxane synthase is the course's example of such specialization. The correct option therefore explains diversity at the downstream conversion stage. PGH2 is not a dead end, and neither exclusive liver COX-1 nor platelet-only arachidonic acid is the basis supplied. Do not read every branch in a generalized diagram as simultaneously active in every cell.

COX-1 and COX-2 are the two PGH-synthase isoforms compared in this course. PLA2 acts earlier, and PGH2 is a product rather than an isoform. Classifying each name by its role helps eliminate these distractors.

The question asks for two enzyme isoforms, so first reject choices that name products or mix an enzyme with a product. COX-1 and COX-2 are the PGHS isoforms used in the lecture's comparison. TxA2 and PGE2 are lipid signals, while PLA2 and PGH2 refer to a different enzyme and an intermediate, respectively. The COX-2/COX-3-only option does not match the two forms emphasized. Distinguishing the isoforms matters because their broad expression patterns and functions help explain both nonselective inhibition and the rationale for COX-2 selectivity.

The course uses COX-1 as the broad constitutive, housekeeping contrast to inducible COX-2. Protective gastric prostaglandins illustrate why inhibiting COX-1 can have unwanted consequences. These are broad teaching distinctions, not a claim that the enzyme exists in only one tissue.

Constitutive means the enzyme is generally present as part of ongoing cellular function in the lecture's broad contrast. COX-1-derived products help support housekeeping roles, including gastric protection. It is therefore not restricted to platelets or described as induced only during inflammation. Aspirin inhibits the relevant enzyme rather than activating it. The wording generally is important: this is the organizing comparison used by the course, not a claim that every tissue follows an absolute on/off rule. The housekeeping role explains why inhibiting COX-1 can also suppress functions that are useful rather than inflammatory.

COX-2 is emphasized as an inducible contributor to inflammatory responses. This explains its connection with inflammatory pain, fever and swelling in the course. It is an enzyme isoform, not a phospholipid or a final signaling product.

The course contrasts inducible inflammatory COX-2 activity with broadly constitutive COX-1 housekeeping activity. COX-2 can be induced in selected cells in response to inflammatory stimuli, contributing to the pathway products associated with pain, fever, and swelling. It is an enzyme isoform, not a membrane phospholipid or the final lipid product. Saying it is absent from inflammatory responses reverses the lecture's emphasis. Preserve the broad comparison without turning it into a universal claim that COX-2 has no roles outside inflammation; the question does not require that stronger statement.

Blocking arachidonic-acid access to the COX catalytic region reduces PGH2 formation and consequently downstream products of this branch. The drugs need not destroy the membrane precursor to achieve this. Stimulating precursor release or TxA2 production would run against the stated effect.

Follow the consequences of blocking substrate access. When arachidonic acid cannot reach the relevant COX catalytic region effectively, less PGH2 is produced. This reduces downstream products of that branch, including the prostaglandins emphasized in the question. Destroying phospholipids or increasing PLA2 activity describes a different, upstream event and is not the inhibition mechanism given here. Stimulating TxA2 would also point in the wrong direction. The explanation concerns the common NSAIDs studied, with selective COX-2 inhibitors treated separately rather than assuming every inhibitor has identical selectivity.

Aspirin modifies the enzyme covalently rather than only occupying a site reversibly. Consequently an inhibited enzyme molecule does not recover simply when free aspirin disappears. That persistence is the distinction the question targets.

Aspirin's distinguishing feature here is covalent modification of COX/PGHS. The lecture describes acetylation of an active-site serine that obstructs substrate access. The inhibited enzyme molecule does not simply recover when unbound drug leaves the surroundings. This contrasts with reversible, noncovalent inhibition by several other NSAIDs in the course. The receptor-antagonist option confuses enzyme inhibition with a different pharmacological mechanism, and activating platelet aggregation is opposite to the TxA2 consequence discussed. Identify the binding chemistry first, then use it to understand why the effect can persist.

Ibuprofen is the reversible-binding comparison in the lecture. Once the noncovalent inhibitor dissociates, the enzyme can regain access to substrate. Aspirin's covalent modification does not behave in that same way.

The contrast is about how the drug interacts with the enzyme, not whether both drugs can reduce pathway activity. Ibuprofen binds noncovalently and reversibly in the course comparison. When a reversible inhibitor dissociates and is removed, its enzyme interaction can end without requiring replacement of a covalently altered enzyme molecule. Aspirin's covalent effect is therefore mechanistically different. Ibuprofen is not converted into TxA2 to perform its role, and its binding is not restricted to anucleate platelets. Keep reversible binding distinct from the prolonged platelet example built around aspirin.

TxA2 is the platelet-derived signal linked to aggregation and vasoconstriction in this pathway. These responses contribute to clot formation. ATP synthesis, glucose uptake and DNA repair do not describe the signaling role being tested.

TxA2 is a downstream lipid signal made through the platelet branch of the pathway. Its effects include promoting platelet aggregation and vasoconstriction, linking the biochemical pathway to early clot-forming processes discussed in the lecture. This is not ATP production, DNA repair, or glucose transport. The question also helps explain the aspirin example: reducing upstream COX activity reduces the PGH2 available for TxA2 formation, which can reduce the aggregating signal. Identify TxA2 as a signaling product rather than the COX enzyme or the membrane precursor.

The effect persists because the enzyme has been covalently modified and the course model emphasizes platelets' limited ability to replace it. Persistence does not require aspirin to remain permanently in plasma. Link the enzyme-level change to continuing reduction of platelet TxA2.

Two facts must be combined. Aspirin covalently inhibits platelet COX, so removal of free drug does not undo that modification. Platelets lack nuclei and cannot readily replace the inhibited enzyme in the way described for nucleated cells in the course model. Reduced COX activity therefore continues to limit PGH2 and TxA2 production after free aspirin has fallen. The explanation is not permanent retention of aspirin in plasma or increased TxA2 synthesis. This is a mechanism question, not a recommendation about who should take aspirin or what dose would be appropriate.

The intended selectivity separates suppression of inflammatory COX-2 activity from preservation of more COX-1 housekeeping activity. It does not imply total elimination of all eicosanoids or freedom from risk. The question concerns the design rationale, not a treatment recommendation.

The intended advantage follows from the course's broad functional contrast. COX-2 inhibition targets the inflammatory contribution, while sparing more COX-1 activity can preserve more housekeeping functions. The lecture explains the possibility of selectivity through a larger access channel in COX-2 that can accommodate a suitably designed inhibitor. This does not imply permanent inhibition of every eicosanoid pathway, activation of PLA2, or deliberate stimulation of TxA2. It also does not establish that a selective drug is risk-free; the source itself notes that selectivity and overall safety are different questions.

Keep pain relief, fever reduction and suppression of local swelling separate. The lecture attributes the first two effects to acetaminophen but does not treat it as a typical peripheral COX inhibitor at the injury site. It leaves the detailed analgesic mechanism uncertain rather than requiring a definitive alternative explanation.

Distinguish a symptom effect from the particular inflammatory mechanism. In this lecture, acetaminophen can reduce pain and fever but is not treated as a typical peripheral COX inhibitor that effectively reduces local injury-site swelling. Pain relief alone therefore does not make it equivalent to the NSAIDs in the course's classification. The covalent-COX option instead describes aspirin's contrast. Do not supply a definitive alternative molecular mechanism to fill the gap: the lecture leaves the detailed analgesic/antipyretic mechanism uncertain. The answer should preserve that uncertainty while explaining the stated difference in effects.

This item explicitly uses the lecture's operational wording: drug present in circulation and available to reach its target. That makes circulating availability the correct concept. It should not be confused with receptor number, a toxic-dose endpoint or cellular ATP production.

The question explicitly uses the lecture's operational meaning: the amount of drug circulating and available to reach its target. Metabolism and excretion can reduce that amount over time, so exposure is not described solely by how much was initially administered. A lethal dose is an endpoint used in a different comparison, and receptor number is not the circulating quantity. ATP production is unrelated to the definition. Use the source's stated terminology here rather than silently replacing it with a different technical pharmacokinetic definition that the question did not ask students to apply.

A half-life describes a halving of concentration, not complete disappearance. Starting from a specified concentration, identify when it reaches one-half of that value. The definition concerns time, unlike therapeutic index, which is a dose ratio.

Half-life describes a proportional decline in concentration, not complete disappearance. As a simple illustration under a constant-half-life assumption, a concentration of 80 arbitrary units would fall to 40 after one half-life and to 20 after another. Those illustrative values show that the second interval halves the remaining amount rather than subtracting the same original amount again. Receptor number and therapeutic index are different quantities. The definition alone does not specify an actual drug's half-life or authorize a dosing decision; it explains the time measure used to describe declining circulating concentration.

The lecture presents Phase I oxidation as part of drug transformation that often facilitates further metabolism and excretion. The direction is toward processing the drug, not a guaranteed increase in half-life. The word often matters: the question does not establish one universal outcome for every compound.

In the course's metabolism sequence, Phase I oxidation often introduces or exposes features that make a compound more water-soluble and suitable for further transformation. Phase II conjugation can then contribute to making it easier to excrete. The word often prevents treating this as a guarantee that every drug behaves identically. Oxidation is not defined as conversion into a lipid or prevention of all conjugation. Nor does it guarantee a longer half-life: metabolism commonly contributes to elimination in this model. Keep the chemical transformation linked to the course's exposure-and-excretion logic.

Place the toxic median dose in the numerator and the effective median dose in the denominator. TI therefore measures their separation as TD50/ED50 under the stated test conditions. Reversing the fraction would reverse the intended interpretation of a larger value.

Read the ratio in words: toxic median dose divided by effective median dose. That gives **TI = TD50/ED50** for the toxic endpoint specified here. Reversing the ratio gives its reciprocal and reverses the intended interpretation of larger values. Multiplying dose by half-life mixes two different quantities, while Km/Vmax is an enzyme-kinetics combination rather than this pharmacological comparison. The dose units must be comparable so they cancel. The result expresses separation between the measured endpoints under the test conditions, not a universal promise about an individual's response.

A larger TI places the median toxic dose farther above the median effective dose, using comparable endpoints and units. That is a wider test-dose margin. It does not prove individual safety or reveal receptor affinity, drug half-life or antagonist status.

A ratio of 1000 means the stated toxic median dose is 1000 times the effective median dose in that comparison, whereas a ratio of 10 gives a much smaller separation. The correct option therefore describes a wider margin between those endpoints. It does not say the drug is ineffective or classify it as an agonist or antagonist. The word generally also matters: a larger therapeutic index is informative about the specified dose comparison, but is not proof of safety for every person, every exposure, or every adverse outcome. The question asks for relative interpretation, not a clinical recommendation.

Both classes can bind receptors; their effect after binding distinguishes them. An agonist activates the response, whereas an antagonist blocks or reduces agonist action without activating that response. Reversing the labels confuses occupancy with signaling.

Use two tests: does the ligand bind, and what happens after binding? Both an agonist and an antagonist can occupy a receptor. An agonist activates the relevant response; an antagonist does not activate that response and interferes with activation by the agonist. Thus binding by itself does not distinguish the categories. The reversed option exchanges their functional definitions, while the no-binding and equal-activation options erase the difference. This distinction is useful when interpreting an experiment: evidence of receptor occupancy must be paired with evidence about the resulting signaling activity.

Use the term in the sense specified by the course, then connect it to removal processes. Metabolism and excretion reduce the circulating amount available over time. This question does not ask you to substitute a different pharmacokinetic definition.

The source uses circulating amount as its operational definition, so the answer should connect drug elimination to that quantity. Metabolism transforms the drug and excretion removes material from the body; in the simplified course account, these processes reduce the circulating amount available over time. That is not the same as therapeutic index, which compares dose endpoints, or receptor number, which concerns the target. The claim that metabolites always remain at the original concentration is unsupported and ignores continuing transformation and removal. Preserve the lecture's exposure-based usage when explaining the answer.

Divide toxic dose by effective dose: 900/30 = 30. The matching dose units cancel, leaving a unitless ratio. This expresses separation between the supplied test doses, not a dosage instruction or a guarantee of safety.

Place the toxic dose in the numerator and the effective dose in the denominator: **TI = 900/30 = 30**. The same dose units appear above and below the division, so the ratio is unitless. A value near 0.033 comes from reversing the ratio; 27000 comes from multiplication; and 870 comes from subtraction. Each performs a different operation from the defined index. The result means a thirty-fold separation between these supplied median-dose endpoints, not that thirty units is a prescribed dose or that every individual is safe below the toxic median.

Sort the similar names by role before choosing: COX/PGHS is the enzyme, PGH2 is its product and TxA2 is a later signal. Aspirin covalently modifies the enzyme. Selecting a lipid product would misidentify the target of inhibition.

Assign the names to a sequence before choosing. Arachidonic acid is the precursor substrate; COX/PGHS is the enzyme; PGH2 is the intermediate it produces; and TxA2 is one possible downstream signal. Aspirin covalently modifies the enzyme, so the target is **COX/PGHS**, not one of the lipid products. The original model answer already documents the source-label inconsistency on slide 11:17. The explanation maintains that documented distinction rather than repeating the confusing label as though enzyme and product were interchangeable. This naming check also supports the platelet mechanism questions.

Upstream PGH2 production does not by itself determine the final signal. Different downstream enzyme sets direct that shared intermediate toward different products. The fourth stage of the course pathway explains the difference between the two cell types.

Both cells have completed the shared upstream part of the pathway because both make PGH2. Their different outcomes must therefore be explained by the later conversion of that intermediate. Cell-specific downstream enzymes direct PGH2 toward different final signals; platelet thromboxane synthase is one example in the course. A generic diagram summarizes possible branches, not a requirement that every cell produce every branch product at the same rate. PGH2 is an intermediate rather than a universal receptor, and replacing arachidonic acid with glycogen would change the pathway incorrectly. Locate the difference at stage four.

The observation separates binding from activation. This ligand occupies the receptor but prevents an activating ligand from generating its response, which fits antagonism. Binding alone is not sufficient evidence that a ligand is an agonist.

The observations provide both the binding and functional information needed for classification. Occupancy shows that the ligand binds. Absence of activation shows that binding alone is insufficient to make it an agonist. Blocking the activating ligand's effect provides the final clue that it acts as an antagonist in this context. A phosphate donor or electron carrier is a different molecular role and does not explain receptor blockade. The answer should refer to the observed response rather than assuming that any ligand recognized by a receptor must turn that receptor's signaling on.

Compare function and inducibility rather than just tissue color. White fat emphasizes storage and endocrine roles, brown fat uses UCP1-rich mitochondria for thermogenesis, and beige fat has inducible thermogenic capacity. Connecting UCP1 to proton return explains the heat-producing functions.

Compare the tissues along two dimensions: their emphasized function and whether thermogenesis is a defining or inducible feature. White adipose tissue primarily stores triacylglycerol and also has endocrine functions. Brown adipose tissue is specialized for heat production and contains many mitochondria with thermogenin/UCP1. Beige adipocytes are distinguished by inducible thermogenesis in the lecture's comparison.

Connect the thermogenic roles to Week 10. UCP1 permits proton return without ATP-synthase capture, shifting more respiratory energy toward heat. This explains the function rather than merely associating colors with different names. The lecture also distinguishes brown fat developmentally, but the question does not require inventing a detailed lineage account. Do not describe white fat as functionless storage or erase the inducibility that distinguishes beige fat in the supplied material.

State the dietary requirement as well as the names. Linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid are essential because synthesis does not meet the requirement described in the course. Useful or abundant is not a sufficient definition of essential.

A complete answer contains the pair, the reason for the dietary requirement, and the omega-family distinction given in the course. The pair is **linoleic acid** and **α-linolenic acid**. They are needed for normal biological function, but the required supply is not met by endogenous synthesis in the account used here. Dietary provision is therefore necessary.

Linoleic acid is omega-6 and α-linolenic acid is omega-3. Their similar names make it worth connecting each name to its family rather than treating them as interchangeable spellings. Essential does not simply mean useful or abundant: many molecules are useful without being nutritionally essential in this sense. Likewise, it does not mean the fatty acid is confined to mitochondria or lacks double bonds. Keep the explanation about the defined dietary requirement rather than adding unsupported nutritional prescriptions.

Start at the methyl end and count to the first double bond. The omega label specifies that position, not the number of double bonds. Explicitly identifying the 3–4 or 6–7 bond makes the naming rule unambiguous.

First identify the terminal methyl end of the fatty-acid chain. Count inward from that end, not from the carboxyl group. In an omega-3 fatty acid, the first double bond encountered is between positions 3 and 4; in omega-6, it is between positions 6 and 7. Stating the pair of positions makes clear which bond the label refers to.

The number is not a count of all double bonds in the molecule. A student who knows that the chain is polyunsaturated still cannot assign its omega family without locating the first double bond relative to the methyl end. Conversely, finding that first bond does not by itself list every other bond position. This is a naming convention about location, so the reference end must be included in a complete explanation.

A complete answer connects chemical origin, family membership and biological roles. The course's detailed COX pathway is one branch within that family. Naming leukotrienes as eicosanoids does not imply that COX makes them through the prostaglandin/TxA2 sequence.

Connect three parts of the definition. The chemical family comprises 20-carbon signals derived from polyunsaturated fatty acids. The categories named by the course include prostaglandins, thromboxanes, leukotrienes, and lipoxins. The functional examples include inflammation, pain, fever, clotting-related responses, and gastric-mucosal regulation.

Then distinguish the broad family from the pathway studied in detail. The PGHS/COX-to-PGH2 sequence supplies the prostaglandin and TxA2 examples, but classifying leukotrienes as eicosanoids does not place them automatically in that same COX branch. This prevents an overgeneralization when interpreting NSAID effects. Also keep products separate from enzymes: an eicosanoid is the lipid-derived signal, not phospholipase A2 or PGHS. The answer should show how origin, category, function, and pathway scope fit together without claiming every cell makes every signal.

Follow precursor release, substrate use, intermediate production and cell-specific conversion in order. The final step explains how cells with a common precursor can produce different signals. Avoid treating every branch in the overview diagram as active in a single cell.

Follow the material through four stages. First, phospholipase A2 releases arachidonic acid from membrane phospholipid. Second, that free precursor becomes the substrate presented to PGHS, represented by the COX-1 and COX-2 isoforms. Third, PGHS generates the unstable intermediate PGH2. Fourth, the cell's downstream enzymes convert that intermediate into particular prostaglandins or TxA2.

The last stage explains cell specificity. A platelet with thromboxane synthase can direct the shared intermediate toward TxA2, while another cell's enzyme set can produce a different outcome. The overview diagram therefore combines potential routes; it is not evidence that all branches operate in every cell.

Keep the similar names attached to their roles throughout: arachidonic acid is substrate, PGHS is enzyme, and PGH2 is product/intermediate. This also makes inhibitor questions easier, because blocking an enzyme upstream changes the supply available to downstream branches rather than directly destroying every final lipid signal.

Arachidonic acid must first be freed from its membrane-phospholipid storage form. Once released, it can serve as substrate for PGHS. This locates the precursor before PGH2 and prevents mixing up a fatty acid with a later intermediate.

The precursor asked for is **arachidonic acid**, but its availability is part of the explanation. Before release, it is commonly esterified within membrane phospholipids rather than existing only as a freely circulating end product. In the illustrated injury-response pathway, phospholipase A2 releases it so it can become substrate for PGHS.

The sequence is therefore membrane phospholipid, released arachidonic acid, and then the PGHS-generated intermediate PGH2. Confusing arachidonic acid with PGH2 moves the answer one stage too far downstream. Confusing it with the enzyme loses the substrate–catalyst distinction. The objective focuses on the specific prostaglandin/TxA2 pathway used in the course, so it should not be expanded into a claim that every lipid signal in every context has an identical immediate precursor or route.

The final letter or number changes the meaning of these similar names. PGHS refers to the enzyme with COX-1 and COX-2 isoforms, while PGH2 names its product. That distinction becomes essential when identifying aspirin's target.

Write the two isoform names as **COX-1 and COX-2**. They are forms of the PGH-synthase enzyme discussed in the lecture, not two downstream eicosanoid products. Their broad expression and functional differences become important when the course considers nonselective versus selective inhibition.

The near-identical labels require particular care: PGHS ends in S for synthase, whereas PGH2 names the intermediate produced. Aspirin modifies the enzyme, while downstream cell-specific enzymes use the intermediate. A useful check is to put each label into a sentence with a verb: PGHS acts on arachidonic acid; PGH2 is formed; later enzymes convert PGH2 into particular signals. That role-based distinction is more robust than trying to distinguish the names by appearance alone.

Connect expression patterns to consequences. Broad housekeeping COX-1 activity explains why its inhibition can remove protective functions; inducible COX-2 activity explains the intended inflammatory effect. Present the comparison at the lecture's broad level rather than converting it into an absolute rule about all tissues.

Use expression pattern to explain function and then inhibition consequences. COX-1 is broadly described as constitutive and contributes to ongoing housekeeping prostaglandin functions, with gastric protection as the course example. COX-2 is described as inducible in selected inflammatory contexts, contributing to pain, fever, and swelling-related signaling.

Inhibition can therefore affect more than one kind of biological activity. Reducing the COX-2 contribution can suppress inflammatory effects, while reducing COX-1 can also interfere with useful housekeeping functions. This is the rationale behind seeking selectivity, not proof that all COX-1 activity is beneficial and all COX-2 activity is harmful. Preserve the lecture's broad contrast without converting it into an absolute rule for every tissue. The question asks for mechanistic comparison, not a clinical ranking of drugs for a particular person.

In the nonselective case, both isoforms can be affected through impaired substrate access. Less PGH2 then means less material for downstream prostaglandin/TxA2 production. Keep COX-2-selective drugs separate from this question's nonselective category.

Trace the blocked event and its consequences. The common nonselective NSAIDs studied occupy or obstruct the COX substrate-access region in both COX-1 and COX-2. This makes it harder for arachidonic acid to reach the catalytic site, reducing the PGH2 supply. Downstream products dependent on that branch can consequently decline.

The mechanism is not destruction of all membrane phospholipids, increased release of precursor by PLA2, or direct elimination of every eicosanoid family. It acts at the specific enzyme step. Both isoforms matter because reducing their activity can affect inflammatory and housekeeping functions in the course's comparison. COX-2-selective inhibitors are discussed separately and should not be forced into the nonselective description. Likewise, aspirin's covalent binding is a further distinction within the inhibitor discussion, not the same binding chemistry as every reversible NSAID.
